speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Earlier this year, CNA screened a documentary titled "Inside Maximum Security".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That documentary featured what inmates go through during their incarceration.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The documentary generated substantial interest in prisons' operations and conditions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Since then, several Members have filed questions on prison conditions and rehabilitation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: From time to time, you will also hear questions on prison conditions in Singapore and whether the conditions ought to be changed.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, Mr Deputy Speaker and Members, I have decided that I will deal with many of those issues by way of a Statement that deals with how our conditions are.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have, both in this House and outside, spoken about the purposes of imprisonment, the outcomes that we aim to achieve, the different types of sentences and the factors taken into account during sentencing.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, this year, in March, during the Committee of Supply (COS) debates and on various other locations.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, I do not intend to repeat those points, but I ask Members to keep those points in mind because they are relevant in understanding our prison regime.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is because you get situations where inmates might try to do a lot of harm to themselves, get contraband, create security situations and other similar issues.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have spoken extensively about this issue as well, previously, including in March of this year during the COS debates, and in earlier years, and so I will not repeat those points.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But as with the other points, the points I made need to be kept in mind as we talk about prison conditions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: My focus today is on the actual conditions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And with your permission, Sir, may I ask that some slides be shown on the LED screens?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is a cell that houses one inmate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members are welcome to visit the prisons for a shorter or longer duration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And now, Members will see the picture of cells that house up to eight inmates, around 20 square metres.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are no fans inside the cells for inmates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They could also be dismantled and the parts potentially used as weapons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Instead, there is a combination of natural and mechanical ventilation inside the cells.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On bedding for inmates, we provide straw mat with two blankets.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Due to our hot and humid climate, mattresses for inmates are not ideal because of hygiene issues, generally.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The current bedding also minimises the security risks of inmates hiding contraband items in the cells.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Generally, there is no direct staff supervision inside the cells.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, beds are provided for inmates who require additional care, such as due to old age or mobility issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, Members can see the photographs of correctional units for assisted living.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These beds are in medical wards as well as the correctional units catered for assisted living that you see in the photos.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These correctional units for assisted living also have other features like seated toilets, handrails, grab bars and anti-slip flooring.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As some would have seen from the CNA documentary, breakfast is bread with spreads like butter, jam or chocolate, and a hot beverage like coffee or tea.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For lunch and dinner, it is a staple such as rice or noodles, with some dishes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, inmates, who are diabetic are given a low sugar diet.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Inmates who have gout are given a low purine diet and vegetarians can request a non-meat diet.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Each inmate is also given basic necessities for daily living: toothbrush, toothpaste, clothing, slippers and towel.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For recreation, inmates have access to electronic tablets in their cells daily.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Tablets are also used to broadcast essential news, information to keep inmates up to date on the latest COVID-19 measures, for example, both within the prison and in the community.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On recreation, inmates typically have at least one hour of out-of-cell recreation on weekdays.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They engage in sports and exercise or read newspapers, play board games or watch TV programmes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are photographs of the common areas and recreational areas that Members can see on the screen.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are conducted either in the recreational yard or day rooms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Staff strength is a consideration as these activities are higher risk and require closer supervision by staff.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some questions have been raised about prison conditions and I will now address them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some Members might remember the case of David James Roach, the perpetrator of the Standard Chartered Bank robbery in 2016.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was claimed then that Singapore's prison conditions would violate his human rights.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He argued this in the UK when arguing against extradition.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: An expert witness for him said that the modesty wall in our prison walls divides the living space from the sanitary facilities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Eating in a cell with a modesty wall does not fully partition the living and sanitation spaces, and it is effectively eating in the toilet.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the mirrored dome on the ceiling of the toilet, which allows prison officers to check on inmates, he said the lack of privacy is not acceptable when inmates use the toilets.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The UK Courts found that while the conditions of our prisons were, in their words, not ideal, the defence counsel representing Roach failed to show that Roach was at real risk of a breach of his rights.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Other points have been made elsewhere about long periods of time inmates spend inside the cell, inmates sleeping on a straw mat and overcrowding.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, the prisons are not overcrowded based on the specifications they were designed for.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For background, I should say overcrowding in prisons is an issue in several countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would be careful with this caveat of comparing the percentages between countries because whether there is overcrowding can be a matter of definition.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It depends on what your baseline is, what your intended capacity of the prison is and how it is designed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the intended capacity of the prison is lower than another, then, of course, occupancy rates would be higher for the first prison, compared with the second, for the same number of inmates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But based on media reports, I think we can say conditions in many of these jails, for example, the US jails, are much worse than ours.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And from what we have seen from photos and media reports, Scandinavian jails are generally much more luxurious.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at a 2021 CBS News report, it describes how overcrowding has led to a deterioration of conditions at Rikers Island prison in New York state.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One New York state lawmaker is quoted as saying that one of the inmate facilities was so overcrowded that prisoners were reported to be staying in rooms without bathrooms for a few hours and some for days.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Another article describes the crowded conditions in New York City's jails as a ticking time bomb.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The head of the Prison Governors Association of the UK, in a report in 2020, said prisoners should be released to reduce overcrowding to prevent disorder and slow the spread, for example, of the COVID-19 virus.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Singapore, the Changi Prison Complex was built in the early 2000s.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are a country of about 733 square kilometres.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is the footprint that we have and we have to maximise the usage of the land.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we want to change it, a huge amount of money will have to be spent, probably running into billions of dollars and with more land taken.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whether that should be done depends on our assessment of the current conditions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our assessment is that conditions are acceptable and fits in with our philosophy of how prisons ought to be.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Essential needs of our inmates are also met.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On medical services: now, all inmates admitted to the prison are assessed on their state of physical and mental health.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Inmates are able to report sick at any time should they feel unwell.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are accorded the necessary medical care by prison medical officers (MOs), prison psychiatrists and supporting medical personnel.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those who require specialist attention and medical care may be referred to Government restructured hospitals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Preventive health measures, including vaccinations, are provided to eligible and willing inmates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, vaccinations against flu, Hepatitis B and, of course, COVID-19.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim has asked about statistics of inmates diagnosed with mental health issues upon admission and the measures to address the needs of inmates who suffer from mental conditions and the support given to such inmates inside prison.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The most common conditions were adjustment disorders and mood disorders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Inmates with mild mental health issues are housed with the general inmate population, seen regularly by the prison psychiatrist and go through rehabilitation programmes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those with severe mental health issues may be housed in a specialised facility, managed with the Institute of Mental Health (IMH), that allows for more intensive intervention and therapy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Inmates who need active IMH follow-ups are referred to a psychiatrist.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Inmates with mental health needs may also have other rehabilitation issues, for example, violent behaviour, that is an increased safety risk for staff and other inmates, and the prisons deals with those.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On feedback, the Singapore Prison Service (SPS) provides various avenues to make inquiries and provide feedback and raise concerns.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They can raise their feedback through their family and friends.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are also independent bodies, like the Board of Visiting Justices comprising prominent members of society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They inspect the prisons; they ensure that the basic well-being of inmates is taken care of, and they hear complaints from inmates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked whether our prison conditions are reflective of SPS' standing as a leading correctional agency.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are countries where prison conditions are less austere than ours.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are also countries where prison conditions are more austere, going to downright extreme overcrowding, as you would have seen from the articles I referred to earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will show Members some photos of prisons in other countries: Denmark, Norway, Thailand, Hong Kong and the Philippines.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at Norway and Denmark, if I did not tell you that was a prison, you might be mistaken for thinking that is a condominium.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our philosophy is to keep the regime strict.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In addition to looking at the physical conditions – and of course, I think many Singaporeans will say we cannot compare with Thailand and the Philippines – but I think Hong Kong is often seen as a fair comparison.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In addition to the actual physical conditions, I would say not enough attention is paid to what I would call the software – the recidivism rate, the effort put into the inmates when they are in prison, the assault rates and whether discipline and inmate safety are maintained.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said, I would call this the software.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What do you do to help the inmates?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How do you make sure they are safe?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our two-year recidivism rates have remained low and stable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prisons is working with the community to improve the five-year recidivism rates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: By comparison, many other countries that you would think of, the two-year recidivism rates are usually in the 40% range, even in places like New Zealand, and the five-year recidivism rates can be in the 60% to 70% range.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we make a real difference to the lives of our inmates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at the assault rate per 10,000 inmates, the assault rate is low.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You look at the big picture and you look at the effort put in.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is another aspect of our prison management that I will like to point out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In some countries, there is a hierarchy among the inmates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some inmates are allowed to exercise control over other inmates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Gangs of inmates are also often allowed to exert their power inside the prisons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You would have seen enough films about this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That includes controlling the underground trade in drugs and other contrabands like cells phones inside the prison.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What happens is that in such prisons, those who are weaker will often be at the mercy of the stronger prisoners.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assault rates between inmates can be quite high.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Inmates who go in, first time, could come out as even more hardened criminals brutalised by the experience.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Their lives are often set on a very sad trajectory from which it is very difficult to change.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the gang situation in our prisons is closely monitored.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do not take me to be saying that some bad things do not happen sometimes in our prisons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We try and maintain safety, order and discipline in our prisons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We want inmates to be focused on rehabilitation and turning their lives around without having to live in constant fear for their personal safety.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members will know how extensive our rehabilitation efforts are.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, I have made several speeches on this, so I will not go into detail.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Instead, I will distribute a document setting out the points in a brief form.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members may also access this annex through the SG PARL MP mobile app.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The rehabilitation approach by Prisons is based on the concept of throughcare – address rehabilitative needs of inmates in prison and facilitate reintegration upon release.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng and Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim had asked about the challenges faced and support for inmates with mental health and medical issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These inmates may face challenges in accessing continual treatment after release, as said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng had asked about the handover of medical care for ex-offenders during this year's Committee of Supply debates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have also set out our approach towards rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am heartened by the good work done by our SPS officers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a volunteer with Yellow Ribbon Singapore, I have visited the prisons myself and spoken to some of the inmates.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have two clarifications: one on the meals for our inmates and second, on the mattresses.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the food, this is a point highlighted to me by a resident as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are three meals for inmates – one for breakfast at 7.30 am, lunch at 12.30 pm and dinner at 6.00 pm.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For inmates who do not have visitors or family members who can provide the approved snack bags by SPS, they would have no choice of any night snacks from the period of 7.00 pm to the following day's breakfast.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would perhaps the Prisons be looking into providing at least some snacks for inmates who require them after 7.30 pm?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Second, on the mattresses, I totally agree with the Minister on the security aspect for hidden contraband risks.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There is also the risk of flammability, I think, of the mattresses.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I quote from the US Consumer Product Safety Commission in this regard that although there are fire-retardant and protective fabric barriers that can be used, through any acts of vandalism, the material within the mattresses can be exposed and be used as a fire safety risk within the prison, posing safety risks for the inmates and our custodians.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it is something that we continue to look at – something that will meet the security requirements and will work in our climate, given that we do not do air conditioning, and that would be resistant to or at least not become a source of passing on disease.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the meals that we provide are based on the recommendations by dieticians.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Any additional amounts that people want, there is a canteen from which they can buy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I should mention that depending on behaviour, good behaviour allows you to certain privileges, including a food pack that you can redeem.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some of my Clementi residents have asked about the ventilation of prison cells that the inmates stay in.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The Minister mentioned that there is natural and mechanical ventilation for these cells.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And secondly, has there been any review or study regarding the risk of transmission of airborne diseases within our prisons, especially in the COVID-19 era.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All our prison institutions are installed with mechanical ventilation systems that are designed to provide sufficient air ventilation into the cells.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are designed to meet the required building standards.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The air changes per hour, which is the number of times the total air volume in a cell is completely removed and replaced in an hour, is regularly monitored to ensure adequate ventilation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Generally, my recollection is that the spread of COVID-19 in prisons was low and the measures taken by Prisons officers – it is not just the physical conditions but the measures we take – were quite adequate to help in that regard.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The first concerns rehabilitation and this is in relation to those who are serving long jail terms – let us say 20 years or more.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Can he confirm whether there is any guideline that the rehabilitation programmes or the reskilling programmes will only be available to these long-term prisoners, perhaps, much closer to their release date, maybe in the one or two years before release, or would they be available to these long-term prisoners even earlier than that?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My second question is, earlier on, the Minister showed a picture of some cells for assisted living, which I believe are for prisoners who are ageing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am taking the second question: as with the rest of society, the general prison population is also ageing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we find more people who need more help.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I cannot give her the precise answer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Perhaps can I ask Ms Lim to file a Parliamentary Question on both those questions that she has raised and we can deal with them in detail?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The first is in relation to the Minister's decision to allow cameras into the prisons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Issues of prison conditions have been raised from time to time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister mentioned that one reason for the austere condition is for the safety of prisoners.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister spoke about the suicide rates are compared to other countries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How about assault rates, compared to other countries?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How does the austere condition allow SPS to reduce opportunities for assaults?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not have the data on this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In some ways, it is due to a variety of reasons which, for example, were raised in the David Roach case, that there is no privacy when one uses the toilet facilities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But a lot of assaults take place there, too, when you give them the privacy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many prisons put prisoners together in a cell; just depend on the number of persons in a cell.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a whole set of infrastructure of factors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I spoke earlier about a hierarchy amongst prisoners.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is a very relevant factor for high assault rates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Singapore, we do not allow any of that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And as a result, prisons officers can intervene fairly quickly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not mean no assaults take place.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sometimes, there are even grievous injuries because people can inflict injuries on one another very, very quickly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you need the right intelligence, you need to know what is going on, who is manoeuvring against whom.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And with the best will in the world and best intelligence, you cannot prevent every incident.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And prisoners committing suicide, it is a big risk.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, monitoring; no gangs; continuous engagement; rehabilitation efforts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But our whole approach is very different and I would say much more focused on trying to make sure that the prisoners are safe and that, when they come out, they are, hopefully, in a better position than when they went in.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We do not always succeed, but that is the aim.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, why did we allow the cameras in prison?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For all these years, it was a taboo.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: No one can go in, which is why I invited Members to turn up as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The approach we decided on was this, that people needed to understand how our prisons operate, what the conditions were.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let the cameras go in, let them speak with the prison inmates themselves, let them speak with the prisons officers so that they understand our approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And this Ministerial Statement, this debate, as it were, is part of that process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For us as a society, we want to set out our approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is how we do it and this is why we do it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are the reasons why we are doing what we are doing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then, if anyone has a different view, we can hear them in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In line with this, I would like to ask whether prisoners are allowed access to newspapers, television or the Internet, and, if so, whether there are any restrictions on this or any security considerations relating to this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The answer is yes, inmates do have access to newspapers and television programmes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They remove contents which depict, describe or may encourage violence, crime or other such conduct.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We also remove articles which may incite social, racial or religious tension.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the newspapers would not be current, what they get.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I find it, I will mention it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I think you can take it as on the record.
